title: Figurative language and multiple-meaning words
blurb: Name the figure of speech, translate it into plain meaning, and pick the sense of a multiple-meaning word that fits this sentence.
question: “The committee voted to table the proposal,” and “For the students, the anatomy final was a mountain.” Neither sentence means what it literally says. How do you work out what each one really means on the TEAS?

teach.body: Literal language means exactly what the words say. Figurative language uses words beyond their literal meaning to create a comparison, an image or an effect. Formally, a figure of speech is a deliberate departure from literal meaning. Plain English: “The waiting room was a zoo” does not mean animals were present; it means the room was crowded and chaotic. Your job is to name the device and translate it into plain meaning.

head: Device
What it does
Example
rows: Her hands were as cold as ice.
A marathon is a bit tiring.

teach.caption: Test for simile first: if “like” or “as” makes the comparison, it is a simile, not a metaphor.

children.label: Verbal
children.sub: says the opposite of what is meant

children.label: Dramatic
children.sub: reader knows what a character does not

children.label: Allusion
children.sub: nod to a known story or figure

teach.h: Scenario: Keisha decodes a student essay
teach.body: Keisha, a nursing applicant, reads this excerpt: “For first-year nursing students, the anatomy final is a mountain. Our study group roped ourselves together for six weeks. The night before the exam, the library clock ticked like a time bomb, and I was sure I had forgotten every bone in the human body. When the scores were posted, I had passed with a 91. My reaction? I was mildly pleased.”

items: “The anatomy final is a mountain”: a direct comparison with no “like.” Metaphor. Plain meaning: the exam is huge and hard to conquer.
“Roped ourselves together”: extends the climbing metaphor. Plain meaning: the students depended on each other.
“Ticked like a time bomb”: a comparison using “like.” Simile. Plain meaning: time was running out and tension was high.
“Forgotten every bone in the human body”: an obvious exaggeration. Hyperbole. Plain meaning: she felt unprepared.
“Mildly pleased” about a 91: deliberately downplayed. Understatement. Plain meaning: she was thrilled.

teach.body: Many words have several dictionary meanings. The TEAS asks for the one that fits THIS sentence, and the trap answer is usually the most common meaning. “The board will table the discussion” means postpone it, not set it on furniture. “A novel approach” means a new approach, not a book. Method: substitute each option into the sentence and keep the one that makes the whole sentence make sense.

head: Sentence
Common meaning
Meaning here
rows: The board will table the vote.
teach.caption: When a familiar word sounds odd in context, that oddness is your clue that another meaning is in play.

teach.text: Two classic traps: reading an idiom or metaphor literally (“under the weather” does not involve rain; “found their footing” does not involve feet), and choosing the most common meaning of a multiple-meaning word instead of the meaning the sentence needs.

items: Simile uses like or as; metaphor compares directly; personification gives human traits to things.
Hyperbole exaggerates; understatement downplays; an idiom is a set phrase with a non-literal meaning.
Irony: verbal (says the opposite), situational (opposite outcome), dramatic (reader knows more).
Oxymoron joins opposites; allusion references a known story; onomatopoeia imitates sounds; alliteration repeats first sounds.
For multiple-meaning words, pick the sense that fits this sentence, not the most common one.

summary: You can now identify similes, metaphors, personification, hyperbole, understatement, idioms, irony, oxymorons, allusions and sound devices, and translate each into plain meaning. You can also choose the in-context sense of a multiple-meaning word rather than its most common one.

A.q: “By 8 a.m. on Monday, the clinic's waiting room was a beehive.” Which figure of speech does this sentence use?
A.why: The sentence says the waiting room WAS a beehive, a direct comparison without “like” or “as.” That is a metaphor.

whyNot.0: A simile needs “like” or “as”; this comparison is stated directly.
whyNot.1: No human trait is given to a nonhuman thing.
whyNot.3: The comparison suggests busy activity rather than exaggerating a quantity, so it is best named a metaphor.

A.q: “After six weeks of practice tests, Marisol passed her certification exam with flying colors and celebrated with her study group.” As used in the sentence, “with flying colors” most nearly means
A.why: “With flying colors” is an idiom meaning with great success, and the celebration supports that reading.

whyNot.1: A narrow pass is the opposite of the idiom's meaning.
whyNot.2: This is the literal reading of the idiom, the classic trap.
whyNot.3: The sentence says nothing about earlier attempts; the idiom describes how well she did.

A.q: “After inspecting the beams and supports, the engineer assured residents that the 80-year-old bridge was still structurally sound.” As used in the sentence, sound most nearly means
A.why: An engineer who inspected beams and supports is judging the bridge's condition. Structurally sound means solid and stable.

whyNot.0: “Audible” links to the most common meaning of sound (a noise), which does not fit a bridge's structure.
whyNot.1: “Sensible” fits phrases like “sound advice,” not the condition of beams and supports.
whyNot.3: Silence has nothing to do with whether the bridge is safe to use.

B.q: After running a marathon in 90-degree heat, Rosa said, “I might be a little thirsty.” Which device is Rosa using?
B.why: After a marathon in extreme heat, she is surely very thirsty; describing it as “a little” deliberately downplays it. That is understatement.

whyNot.0: Hyperbole exaggerates; Rosa does the opposite.
whyNot.1: An oxymoron joins two opposite words, such as “deafening silence.”
whyNot.2: Personification gives human traits to a nonhuman thing; Rosa is describing her own thirst.

B.q: “The hospital's old freight elevator groaned and complained its way up to the fourth floor.” What does the personification suggest about the elevator?
options: Its riders were unhappy with it
It moved slowly and with strain
It was noisy but unusually fast
B.why: Giving the elevator human actions (groaning, complaining) suggests it struggled: slow, strained and noisy.

whyNot.0: The human actions belong to the elevator, not its riders; this reads the device too literally.
whyNot.2: Groaning and complaining its way up suggests effort and slowness, not speed.
whyNot.3: An “old” elevator that groans suggests wear, not a recent repair.

B.q: “The city's new anti-littering billboard was blown down in a storm, and its pieces lay scattered across the park for weeks.” Which type of irony does this illustrate?
B.why: A sign meant to stop litter became litter: the outcome is the opposite of what was expected. That is situational irony.

whyNot.0: Verbal irony is a speaker saying the opposite of what they mean; no one speaks here.
whyNot.2: Dramatic irony requires the reader to know something a character does not.
whyNot.3: No comparison between unlike things is made; the sentence reports an ironic event.

C.q: “In her first weeks on the cardiac unit, Dana felt as if she were drinking from a fire hose. By her third month, though, she had learned the ropes and could anticipate what each patient needed before being asked.” As used in the passage, “learned the ropes” most nearly means
C.why: “Learned the ropes” is an idiom meaning learned how a job is done. The proof is in the passage: she could anticipate each patient's needs.

whyNot.0: This reads the idiom literally; nothing in the passage involves actual ropes.
whyNot.1: She stayed on the cardiac unit and improved there; no transfer is mentioned.
whyNot.3: This reverses the meaning: anticipating patients' needs shows growing skill, not fatigue.

C.q: “After two days of observation, the patient was discharged with instructions to rest and drink plenty of fluids.” As used in the sentence, discharged most nearly means
C.why: A patient sent home after observation with home-care instructions has been released from the hospital.

whyNot.1: Being let go from a job is a common meaning of discharge that does not fit a patient.
whyNot.2: Discharge can mean fluid released from the body, but the instructions to rest at home point to release from care.
whyNot.3: An electrical discharge has nothing to do with a patient going home.

C.q: “On flu-shot day, the clinic ran on a kind of organized chaos, and somehow 400 patients were vaccinated in six hours.” The phrase “organized chaos” is an example of
C.why: “Organized” and “chaos” are opposites placed side by side. Joining contradictory words is an oxymoron.

whyNot.0: Alliteration repeats beginning sounds; “organized” and “chaos” start with different sounds.
whyNot.1: Hyperbole exaggerates; the phrase joins opposite ideas, and 400 patients is presented as a real count.
whyNot.2: An idiom is a set phrase whose meaning cannot be worked out from its words, such as “under the weather.”

reteach.title: Translate the text message
reteach.question: Your friend texts: “This shift is killing me. The manager is a dragon today. I'm dead on my feet.” Nobody is dying and there is no dragon. You already translate figurative language every day.

blocks.body: “Killing me” is hyperbole: the shift is exhausting. “The manager is a dragon” is a metaphor: the manager is fierce. “Dead on my feet” is an idiom: extremely tired. You never pictured a dragon; you went straight to the plain meaning. On the TEAS, do the same thing, and also name the device you translated.

blocks.text: If an answer choice describes the literal picture (an actual dragon, actual feet), it is the trap. The TEAS wants the plain meaning behind the picture.

explain.body: Both compare two unlike things. A simile uses “like” or “as” (“ran like a deer”). A metaphor states the comparison directly (“the lobby was a beehive”). Personification gives human traits to nonhuman things (“the engine coughed”).

test.q: “The nurse's calm voice was like warm honey to the frightened child.” Which device does this sentence use?
test.why: The comparison between the voice and warm honey is made with “like,” so it is a simile.

whyNot.0: A metaphor compares directly, without “like” or “as.”
whyNot.1: No human trait is given to a nonhuman thing; the voice belongs to a person.
whyNot.2: Onomatopoeia uses words that imitate sounds, such as “buzz.”

explain.body: Hyperbole exaggerates for effect (“I've told you a million times”). Understatement makes something seem smaller than it is (“a bit of a scratch” for a deep cut). An idiom is a fixed phrase whose meaning differs from its words (“under the weather”).

test.q: “My backpack weighs a ton after I pack all my anatomy textbooks.” What does the hyperbole convey?
options: The backpack feels very heavy to carry
The textbooks are written in great detail
test.why: “Weighs a ton” exaggerates for effect; the plain meaning is that the backpack feels very heavy.

whyNot.0: This reads the exaggeration literally, which is the classic trap.
whyNot.2: The sentence is about weight, not the content of the books.
whyNot.3: Nothing expresses dislike of the subject; the complaint is about weight.

explain.body: Verbal irony says the opposite of what is meant. Situational irony is an outcome opposite to what was expected. Dramatic irony is when the reader knows something a character does not. Onomatopoeia imitates sounds (beep, sizzle); alliteration repeats first sounds (“busy, bustling ward”).

head: Irony type
Clue
rows: Reader knows more than a character

test.q: In a short story, readers know that Maria's coworkers are hiding in the break room for a surprise party, but Maria walks down the hall believing everyone has forgotten her birthday. This is an example of
test.why: The reader knows about the party while Maria does not. That gap in knowledge is dramatic irony.

whyNot.0: Situational irony is an unexpected outcome; here the point is what the reader knows and Maria does not.
whyNot.1: No one says the opposite of what they mean.
whyNot.3: No one downplays anything in words.

explain.body: Choose the meaning that fits this sentence. The trap is the most familiar meaning. Substitute each option and keep the one that makes the whole sentence work.

test.q: “Lawmakers hope the new rules will check the rapid rise in prescription drug prices over the next five years.” As used in the sentence, check most nearly means
test.why: Rules aimed at a “rapid rise” are meant to hold it back. In this context, check means limit or restrain.

whyNot.1: “Inspect” is the most common meaning of check, but rules cannot inspect a price rise.
whyNot.2: Checking items off a list records them, but that meaning does not fit slowing a rise.
whyNot.3: A check can be a way to pay, but lawmakers are trying to slow prices, not pay them.
